extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of American journalism history; readers interested in the development of early U.S. newspapers
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting criteria and standards apparent in a historical account for assessing the quality, role, and survival of newspapers and magazines in the U.S. (1783–1801). Useful for judging editorial, financial, legal, and production aspects of early press outlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partisan alignment / party organ
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a paper serves as the organ of a political party or administration (e.g., Federalist or Republican), openly declaring or effectively acting as a party champion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Aurora, Porcupine’s Gazette, Columbian Centinel. Being the administration's organ (or failing to become one) determined national leadership and influence; explicit professions of impartiality were often discarded in favor of partisan advocacy ('Professions of impartiality I shall make none').

rubrics_metrics.name: National leadership and influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Capacity of a paper to achieve leadership beyond its city or region and to shape national political debate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A paper that became 'the organ of the new administration' or produced widely copied summaries and arguments (e.g., Russell’s Centinel) was recognized as a leading Federalist champion. Loss of geographic advantage (e.g., capital moving) could undercut national leadership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial style and tone
rubrics_metrics.description: The character of the paper's rhetoric — vituperative invective, satire, lampoon, personal abuse, or measured argument — and how that style affects reputation and effectiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cobbett’s 'extremely vituperative style' and 'billingsgate' could be powerful but led to disrepute and libel. A biting, satirical tone could make a paper effective short-term ('tongue-lashing fishwife') but risked legal and reputational costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Financial viability and patronage
rubrics_metrics.description: Economic sustainability through advertising patronage, sales (circulation), and government patronage or printing contracts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many partisan papers 'lost money' and relied on advertising; government patronage (printing contracts, post office appointments) could be decisive. Failure to secure patronage (Duane’s disappointment) or adverse taxes could force discontinuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal vulnerability (libel and litigation risk)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exposure to libel suits, criminal or civil penalties, and other legal reprisals for published statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Porcupine’s Gazette suffered a $5,000 verdict for libeling Dr. Benjamin Rush; libel trials could be ruinous (trial costs, arrests, editors fleeing). Excessive personal abuse and slander were clear anti-patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: News gathering and editorial quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Skill in collecting, summarizing, and presenting news and editorial material — e.g., original summaries rather than blind copying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Russell’s 'admirable summaries' of foreign news were copied by other papers and enhanced esteem; excellence in both news content and advertising contributed to a paper’s standing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content mix (foreign, governmental, local, literary, advertising)
rubrics_metrics.description: Balance of foreign and governmental intelligence, local news, literary miscellany, and advertising in a paper’s columns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Country papers typically emphasized foreign/governmental intelligence, had very little local news, included some literary pieces, and filled pages with local ads. That composition was characteristic of the period and expected by readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format and publication frequency innovations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of publication strategies such as semiweekly/weekly 'country editions', weekly magazines, or changing format to reach new markets or avoid constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'semiweekly or weekly edition for country readers' recycled daily content cheaply and profitably. Some papers changed to magazine format to evade stamp taxes; innovations expanded circulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical production and visual quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Material appearance and technical production: paper stock, printing quality, illustrations, page counts, and type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Columbian Magazine was noted as the 'handsomest' with elaborate copperplate engraving; conversely, poor paper and bad printing degraded a paper’s appearance and reception ('appearance declined rapidly... poor paper and bad printing').

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary content and magazine character
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence and quality of essays, satire, poetry, apologues, and other literary material that give a periodical broader cultural prestige.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Joseph Dennie’s 'Lay Preacher' essays elevated the Farmer’s Weekly Museum and extended circulation beyond its locale; strong literary content could make a paper 'in fact a Magazine in a minor form.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality versus compilation ('scissors and paste-pot')
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree to which a paper or magazine produces original material versus relying on reprinting and compilation from other papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many magazines were 'scrapbookish miscellanies' assembled from other sources; originality (e.g., original essays, summaries) increased distinction, while reprinting was common and accepted as normal practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution and logistical capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical ability to obtain supplies, print, and distribute a paper — including transport of presses, availability of paper, postal routes, and local infrastructure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pittsburgh Gazette's press had to be brought across the Alleghenies; shortages of supplies occasionally forced improvisation (borrowing cartridge-paper); the setting up of a paper mill and postal routes improved distribution and viability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of the press and access to official proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal and practical freedom to report, discuss, and publish debate (including access to legislative galleries and constitutional/state guarantees).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Senate opened its galleries to the press after complaints; state constitutions often included press guarantees while the federal Constitution initially did not. Threats to freedom included stamp taxes, advertising taxes, and indirect control via government contracts or post office favoritism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial independence versus government influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Extent to which a paper maintains independence from government influence, directly or indirectly (through printing contracts, patronage, post office privileges).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poverty of printers made some susceptible to indirect control; state printing contracts and government patronage could influence editorial positions. Excessive dependence on such patronage was an anti-pattern for independent journalism.
